rewritten_text:
Day was breaking when I put down the manuscript. The rain had nearly stopped; the world looked gray and sorrowful, and the spent storm sighed and sobbed its way into silence. I went to the stranger’s room and listened outside his door, which stood a little open. Hearing his voice, I knocked. No reply came, though the voice continued. I glanced inside. He lay on his back, speaking in fragments but with animation, his arms supplying emphasis as he flung them restlessly about like a feverish patient. I entered quietly and leaned over him. His murmurs and sudden exclamations continued. I said a single word, merely to draw his attention. At once his glazed eyes and ashen face brightened with delight, gratitude, joy, and welcome:

“Oh, Sandy, you have come at last—how I’ve yearned for you! Sit beside me—don’t go—never leave me again, Sandy, never again. Where is your hand? Give it to me, darling, let me hold it—there—now everything is right, everything is peaceful, and I’m happy once more—we’re happy once more, aren’t we, Sandy? You look so faint, so indistinct, only a mist, a cloud, yet you are here, and that is happiness enough; and I’m holding your hand. Don’t pull it away—it will only be a little while; I won’t need it long.... Was that our child? ... Hello-Central! ... She makes no answer. Sleeping, perhaps? Bring her here when she wakes; let me feel her hands, her face, her hair, and say farewell.... Sandy! Yes, you’re still there. For a moment I wandered, and I thought you had left.... Have I been ill a long time? I must have been; it feels like months. And the dreams! Such terrible, peculiar dreams, Sandy! Dreams every bit as real as life—delirium, naturally, but so real! Why, I imagined the king had died, that you were in Gaul and unable to return, that a revolution had broken out. In the fantastic madness of those dreams, I thought Clarence and I, with a few of my cadets, had fought and wiped out the entire knighthood of England! Yet even that wasn’t the strangest thing. I seemed to belong to a distant age not yet born, hundreds of years ahead, and that seemed as true as anything else! Yes, I thought I had flown backward from that age into ours, then forward into it again, and been left friendless and a stranger in that unfamiliar England, with a gulf of thirteen centuries opening between you and me! Between me and my home, my friends! Between me and everything I love, everything that could make life worth living!”

Mr. Wickham found this conversation so thoroughly satisfying that he never again troubled himself, or irritated his dear sister Elizabeth, by raising the subject. She was glad to discover that she had said enough to silence him.

Soon the day arrived for him and Lydia to leave. Mrs. Bennet had to accept a separation likely to last at least a year, since her husband refused to support her plan for the whole family to go to Newcastle.

“Oh, my dear Lydia,” she cried, “when will I see you again?”

“Oh, goodness! I don’t know. Perhaps not for another two or three years.”

“Write to me very often, my dear.”

“As often as I can. But you know married women have very little time for letters. My sisters can write to me. They won’t have anything else to do.”

Mr. Wickham said goodbye much more affectionately than his wife. He smiled, looked handsome, and delivered plenty of charming remarks.

“He is as splendid a fellow as I’ve ever encountered,” said Mr. Bennet once they had left the house. “He simpers, he smirks, and he courts every one of us. I am enormously proud of him. I challenge even Sir William Lucas to present a more valuable son-in-law.”

Her daughter’s departure left Mrs. Bennet listless for several days.

“I often think,” she said, “that nothing is worse than parting from the people one loves. One feels so abandoned without them.”

“That is what happens when you marry off a daughter, Mama,” Elizabeth replied. “It ought to make you more content that your other four remain single.”

“It does nothing of the kind. Lydia isn’t leaving because she is married, but because her husband’s regiment happens to be stationed so far away. If it were closer, she wouldn’t have left so soon.”

But news soon began to circulate that lifted her out of the despondency caused by this event and filled her mind once more with the restlessness of hope. Netherfield’s housekeeper had been instructed to prepare for her master’s arrival. He would return in a day or two and spend several weeks shooting there. Mrs. Bennet could hardly sit still. She alternately looked at Jane, smiled, and shook her head.

“Well, well, so Mr. Bingley is coming back, sister,” she said, for Mrs. Philips had brought her the news. “Well, all the better. Not that it matters to me. He means nothing to us, you know, and I certainly never want to see him again. Still, he is perfectly welcome to come to Netherfield if he wishes.”

The two ladies expressed great pleasure at seeing their dear friend again, declared that ages had passed since their last meeting, and asked again and again how she had occupied herself in the meantime. They scarcely noticed the other members of the family, keeping as far from Mrs. Bennet as they could, addressing little to Elizabeth and nothing whatever to the rest. Their visit soon ended. They sprang from their chairs with an energy that surprised their brother and hurried away as though anxious to evade Mrs. Bennet’s attentions.

Every woman in the family found the thought of the Netherfield ball exceedingly pleasing. Mrs. Bennet elected to regard it as an entertainment in her eldest daughter’s honor, and felt especially gratified that Mr. Bingley had delivered the invitation himself rather than sending a formal card. Jane imagined a delightful evening with her two friends and their attentive brother. Elizabeth looked forward to numerous dances with Mr. Wickham, and to finding confirmation of all she had heard in Mr. Darcy’s expression and conduct. Catherine and Lydia expected happiness less from any particular occurrence or individual. Though each intended, like Elizabeth, to spend half the evening dancing with Mr. Wickham, he was hardly the only partner capable of pleasing them, and a ball, after all, was a ball. Even Mary assured the family that she felt no aversion to attending.

“So long as my mornings remain my own,” she said, “I require nothing further. I see no sacrifice in taking part occasionally in evening parties. Society makes demands upon every one of us, and I count myself among those who believe that periods of relaxation and diversion are beneficial to all.”

Elizabeth was in such excellent spirits that, although she seldom addressed Mr. Collins without necessity, she could not resist asking whether he meant to accept Mr. Bingley’s invitation, and, if so, whether he thought it appropriate to participate in the evening’s entertainment. She was somewhat astonished to learn that he had no reservations on that score, and did not remotely fear that either the Archbishop or Lady Catherine de Bourgh would reprimand him for daring to dance.

“I assure you that I do not in the least believe,” he said, “that such a ball, offered by a young gentleman of good character to respectable company, can exert any harmful influence. Indeed, far from objecting to dancing on my own account, I hope to enjoy the honor of partnering each of my fair cousins during the evening. I therefore take this occasion to request your hand, Miss Elizabeth, particularly for the first two dances; a distinction which I trust my cousin Jane will ascribe to its proper motive, and never to any want of respect toward herself.”
